article_title: ESLint Ships Official Shell Script Linting Plugin, Extending Its Multi-Language Push With ShellCheck-Inspired Rules

content_preview.title: ESLint Ships Official Shell Script Linting Plugin, Extending Its Multi-Language Push With ShellCheck-Inspired Rules
content_preview.summary: ESLint's new official @eslint/shell plugin adds ShellCheck-inspired rules for Bash, POSIX sh and mksh scripts, extending a push that already covers JSON, Markdown and CSS.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

ESLint now officially supports linting shell scripts, according to the [ESLint blog](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/), which announced the `@eslint/shell` plugin on November 6, 2026. The post frames the release as "another step towards providing a language-agnostic platform for source code linting," noting that ESLint had previously added official support for JSON, Markdown, and CSS since outlining that broader goal, according to the [ESLint blog](h...

editor_notes.source_verification: Context: a prior submission on this exact topic (PR for 'ESLint Adds an Official Shell Script Linting Plugin...', submission 2026-11-20T12-33-44Z) was REJECTed for a pattern of quote-fidelity failures: one fully fabricated quote attributed to github.com/mvdan/sh, a quote misattributed to the wrong cited source, two altered quotes from the blog, and a spliced closing quote with four separate alterations, plus a rule-count error (claimed 10 but body text said 11 elsewhere) and only 9 of 10 rules enumerated. This is a materially different submission (different submission timestamp/hash/signature, re-researched, no mvdan/sh source used at all) on a story that never published, so it is not a duplicate review of merged content. Applied maximum scrutiny given that history. All 3 sources fetched successfully (status 200, no suspicious_patterns in manifest.json) and re-verified by decompressing each .html.gz and rehashing against manifest sha256 — all three matched exactly (source-0: db2798ac..., source-1: 802399e7..., source-2: 56af8556...). source-0.html.gz (eslint.org blog, 'ESLint now officially supports linting of shell scripts', published/updated 06 Nov 2026, byline Nicholas C. Zakas / ESLint Technical Steering Committee) — read in full as extracted plain text; confirms the July 2024 general-purpose-linter plan, prior JSON/Markdown/CSS support, the @eslint/shell introduction, Bash/POSIX/mksh dialect support, ESTree-style tree, mvdan-sh/shfmt parser lineage, inline-disable-comment example, and the byline/date. source-1.html.gz (github.com/eslint/shell README, full rule table) — read in full; confirms npm install command ('npm install --save-dev eslint @eslint/shell'), Node requirement '^20.19.0 || ^22.13.0 || >=24', 'Tested with ESLint v10', the three languages (shell/bash used by recommended config, shell/posix, shell/mksh), and critically the 10-row rule table: no-backticks/SC2006/fixable/error, no-expansions-in-single-quotes/SC2016/warn, no-ls-iteration/SC2045/error, no-unquoted-expansions/SC2086-46/fixable/error, no-unused-vars/SC2034/error, no-useless-cat/SC2002/error, no-useless-echo/SC2116/error, no-variables-in-printf-format/SC2059/error, require-cd-guard/SC2164/error, require-read-r/SC2162/fixable/error — exactly 10 rules, exactly as the article enumerates them, and no-expansions-in-single-quotes is indeed the only 'warn'-level rule as the article states. source-2.html.gz (github.com/eslint/shell/releases) — read in full; confirms v0.1.0 released 03 Nov 22:10 2026, v0.1.1 released 06 Nov 21:22 2026, v0.1.2 released 06 Nov 21:39 2026 (17 minutes apart, both same day as the blog post) — matches the article's claims of '0.1.0 on November 3... three days before the public announcement' and '0.1.1 and 0.1.2... tagged minutes apart on November 6... the same day as the blog post.' Minor observation (not a correction): the v0.1.0 release notes list all 10 rules as added in that initial release (0.1.1/0.1.2 are bug-fix-only releases), so the breakdown the article's 'What We Don't Know' section says the blog post doesn't specify is in fact determinable from the releases page the article itself cites elsewhere — the sentence is narrowly and accurately scoped to 'the blog post' specifically so it is not a false statement, but it slightly undersells information available from the Herald's own other cited source. Not corrections-worthy on its own. Anthropic disclosure: not required - the article's subject is ESLint's shell-linting plugin; Anthropic, Claude Code, and Bun are not the subject, headline, summary, or lead, and contributor_model (Claude Sonnet 5) is pipeline metadata, not an in-article credit line.
editor_notes.quote_audit: Exhaustive check of every "..." string in body_markdown (9 total) against the raw decompressed source-0.html.gz text, word-for-word: (1) 'another step towards providing a language-agnostic platform for source code linting' = verbatim match to the blog's subtitle 'Taking another step towards providing a language-agnostic platform for source code linting.' (trailing punctuation adapted from period to comma to fit the citing sentence, standard practice, no words changed). (2) 'an officially supported language plugin for ESLint' = verbatim match to 'The @eslint/shell plugin is an officially supported language plugin for ESLint.' (3) 'provides parsing for shell scripts, a set of rules inspired by ShellCheck, and a recommended configuration' = verbatim match, same sentence continuation, including the period. This is the exact point where the REJECTED prior submission misattributed GitHub-README-only wording ('ShellCheck checks') to this source — the new submission correctly omits 'checks' and matches the blog exactly. (4) 'languages' (bare term, no attribution) = consistent with README section header 'Languages' and blog's plugin-architecture description; not a disputed verbatim claim. (5) 'built on `mvdan-sh`, the parser used by `shfmt`' = verbatim match to 'The parser is built on mvdan-sh, the parser used by shfmt.' This is also the exact claim area where the prior REJECTED submission fabricated an entire quote by citing github.com/mvdan/sh directly; this submission avoids that failure mode entirely by dropping mvdan/sh as a source and sourcing the claim only to the blog post, where it is verbatim. (6) 'ESTree-style syntax tree' = verbatim match to 'parses shell scripts into an ESTree-style syntax tree' (also verbatim in the GitHub README). (7) 'uses Bash and enables rules that catch common problems, such as unquoted expansions, unused variables, and unsafe `read` usage' = verbatim match, including 'catch' (not 'catching' as the prior rejected draft had altered it). (8) 'an important part of many projects, from build and release automation to local development tools' = verbatim match to 'Shell scripts are an important part of many projects, from build and release automation to local development tools.' (9) 'lint shell scripts alongside the rest of your code using ESLint's configuration system and familiar rule APIs' = verbatim match to 'you can lint shell scripts alongside the rest of your code using ESLint's configuration system and familiar rule APIs.' Quotes 8 and 9 are the two halves of what the REJECTED prior submission spliced into a single altered quote (dropping 'and familiar rule APIs', substituting 'users'/'other code' for 'you'/'the rest of your code', truncating without an ellipsis); this submission correctly restructures them as two separately-attributed, independently verbatim quotes as the writer's self-report claimed. All 9 quotes verified verbatim with no fabrication, no misattribution, and no undisclosed alteration. The writer's self-reported fixes (wrong release date caught and corrected to Nov 6 2026 matching the blog's 'Published 06 Nov, 2026'; rule count corrected from an earlier 11 to the verified 10; completeness gap fixed by enumerating all 10 rules matching the README table; compound quote split into two verbatim, separately-attributed quotes) all independently verify as present and correct in the final submitted text — none of this was taken on the writer's word alone.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All substantive claims (release date, dialect support, install/compatibility requirements, parser lineage, rule count and content, release-tag timeline, license/credit) trace to the cited sources and were independently re-derived from raw source text, not accepted from the writer's self-report. No hallucinated specifics found. The 'ten rules' claim and all ten rule descriptions were checked individually against the GitHub README's rule table and match exactly, including which single rule is 'warn' rather than 'error' and which rules are auto-fixable.
